BW JUICE AND BAR RESTAURANT — Complete Website Development Plan

You want to develop a website for BW JUICE AND BAR RESTAURANT where customers can view the menu, select food and drinks, add items to a cart, and place orders online. The restaurant owner and staff should also have an admin dashboard to manage menus and orders.

I recommend building it as a full-stack restaurant ordering system, not just a static website. This means the frontend, backend, database, and ordering process work together.

1. What the website will look like

The website will have two main areas:

  • Customer website: Customers browse the menu and order food, juice, and drinks.

  • Admin dashboard: Authorized staff manage menu items, prices, orders, availability, and restaurant information.

2. Recommended technology stack

Since you want to build a functional web application, I recommend React with TypeScript for the frontend and Express with TypeScript for the backend.

Frontend — React + TypeScript + Vite

Build the homepage, menu, cart, checkout, order tracking, login, and responsive user interface.

Backend — Node.js + Express + TypeScript

Handle authentication, order processing, menu management, validation, and business rules.

Database — MongoDB

Store menu items, customer accounts, orders, prices, and restaurant settings.

Styling — Pure CSS

Create the design without Tailwind CSS, Bootstrap, or Material UI.

Additional tools:

  • React Router — page navigation.

  • Axios or Fetch API — frontend-to-backend communication.

  • JWT and bcrypt — authentication and password security.

  • Mongoose — MongoDB data models.

  • Git and GitHub — source control.

  • Vercel for the frontend and Render for the backend — deployment options.

3. Customer website pages

1. Home page

  • BW JUICE AND BAR RESTAURANT logo.

  • Navigation: Home, Menu, About, Contact, My Orders.

  • Attractive hero section with food and juice photography.

  • Buttons: Order Now and Explore Menu.

  • Popular items, special offers, opening hours, location, and footer.

2. Menu page

Customers browse items by category, search by name, filter by category, and view prices and availability.

Example categories:

  • Fresh Juices

  • Smoothies and Milkshakes

  • Coffee and Tea

  • Breakfast and Snacks

  • Meals and Fast Food

  • Other Beverages

3. Shopping cart

  • Add and remove menu items.

  • Increase or decrease quantity.

  • Display item prices and subtotal.

  • Calculate applicable delivery fees and total.

  • Keep the cart when the customer navigates between pages.

4. Checkout page

Collect the customer's name, phone number, order type, and relevant details.

Customers select:

  • Dine-in, takeaway, or delivery.

  • Table number for dine-in, or address for delivery.

  • Available payment method.

  • Optional order instructions.

The server validates the order before saving it.

5. My Orders page

Customers can view order numbers, ordered items, totals, order dates, and current status.

Example statuses: Pending, Confirmed, Preparing, Ready, Completed, and Cancelled.

6. About and Contact pages

Show the restaurant's story, address, phone number, opening hours, social media links, and contact information.

4. Admin dashboard modules

The admin dashboard is the control center for the restaurant. It must be protected by authentication and role-based permissions.

Dashboard overview

Today's orders, sales, pending orders, popular products, and low-stock or unavailable items.

Menu management

Create, edit, delete, search, and categorize menu items. Set prices, upload images, and mark products available or unavailable.

Order management

View new orders, confirm orders, update preparation status, cancel with a reason, and mark completed orders.

Customer management

View customer information and order history. Limit access to sensitive information.

Sales and reports

Daily and monthly sales, order counts, top-selling products, and downloadable reports.

Restaurant settings

Business name, logo, contact details, opening hours, delivery fee, currency, and password management.

Optional modules for a later version include ingredient inventory, staff accounts, discount codes, customer reviews, reservations, and kitchen display screens. Do not build everything at once; first make the ordering process reliable.

5. How the ordering process works

This is the most important part of the system.

1. Customer selects a product

For example, a mango juice and a sandwich.

2. Customer adds items to cart

Quantity and estimated total are displayed.

3. Customer submits checkout

Contact information, order type, and payment option are submitted.

4. Backend validates and saves order

Checks product IDs, current prices, availability, quantities, and order details.

5. Admin or staff receives the order

The order appears in the dashboard for confirmation and preparation.

6. Staff updates the order status

Confirmed → Preparing → Ready → Completed.

Critical rule: Never trust the price sent by the frontend. The backend must look up the current price from the database and calculate the final total. Otherwise, customers could manipulate prices in their browser.

For a first version, the simplest approach is to accept orders and allow the restaurant to confirm them manually. Later, add real-time notifications and online payments.

6. Database design

MongoDB can store the following collections.

Collection

Main information

users

Name, email or phone, password hash, role

categories

Category name, description, image

menuItems

Name, description, category, price, image, availability

orders

Order number, customer, items, total, order type, status

payments

Payment method, amount, reference, verification status

reviews

Customer, rating, comment, moderation status

settings

Restaurant details, hours, currency, fees

For every order, save a snapshot of each ordered item's name, unit price, and quantity. This preserves historical order details even if the menu price changes later.

Example order:

JSON
{
  "orderNumber": "BW-1001",
  "items": [
    {
      "name": "Mango Juice",
      "unitPrice": 120,
      "quantity": 2
    }
  ],
  "subtotal": 240,
  "deliveryFee": 0,
  "total": 240,
  "orderType": "takeaway",
  "status": "pending",
  "paymentStatus": "unpaid"
}

This is an illustrative record, not a real order. The sample price is not a recommended restaurant price, and the final implementation should use the restaurant's actual currency and menu prices.

7. Backend API endpoints

The React application will communicate with Express through API endpoints such as these:

Endpoint

Public endpoints should only expose appropriate public information. Admin endpoints must verify the user's identity and permissions on the server. Hiding admin buttons in React is not sufficient security.

8. Recommended project folder structure

Create two separate folders: one for the frontend and one for the backend.

Plain text
BW-JUICE-AND-BAR/ │ ├── frontend/ │ ├── public/ │ └── src/ │ ├── assets/ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── Navbar.tsx │ │ ├── Footer.tsx │ │ ├── MenuCard.tsx │ │ └── CartItem.tsx │ ├── pages/ │ │ ├── Home.tsx │ │ ├── Menu.tsx │ │ ├── Cart.tsx │ │ ├── Checkout.tsx │ │ ├── MyOrders.tsx │ │ ├── Login.tsx │ │ └── admin/ │ │ ├── Dashboard.tsx │ │ ├── ManageMenu.tsx │ │ ├── ManageOrders.tsx │ │ └── Reports.tsx │ ├── services/ │ │ └── api.ts │ ├── context/ │ │ └── CartContext.tsx │ ├── types/ │ ├── App.tsx │ ├── main.tsx │ └── index.css │ ├── backend/ │ └── src/ │ ├── config/ │ │ └── database.ts │ ├── models/ │ │ ├── User.ts │ │ ├── MenuItem.ts │ │ ├── Category.ts │ │ └── Order.ts │ ├── controllers/ │ ├── routes/ │ ├── middleware/ │ ├── services/ │ ├── utils/ │ └── server.ts │ ├── README.md └── .gitignore

For maintainability, give every page and reusable component its own CSS file as the project grows, for example Menu.tsx with Menu.css. Keep shared design variables in index.css.

9. Website design and user experience

I recommend a fresh, premium juice-bar design rather than a generic restaurant template.

Fresh and colorful

Use bright fruit photography and warm orange accents.

Clean and premium

Use white or cream backgrounds, dark readable text, and generous spacing.

Mobile-friendly

Make the menu and checkout easy to use on phones.

Staff-friendly dashboard

Make new orders and order status changes easy to see.

Suggested design system:

  • Primary color: orange.

  • Secondary color: fresh green.

  • Background: white or warm cream.

  • Text: dark charcoal.

  • Buttons: rounded corners, clear labels, and visible hover states.

  • Menu cards: product photo, name, short description, price, availability, and Add to Cart button.

  • Responsive layouts: desktop, tablet, and mobile.

Do not use so many animations or colors that the ordering process becomes confusing. Fast ordering is more important than decorative effects.

10. Authentication, payments, and security

These features need to be designed correctly from the beginning.

Authentication

  • Admin login with a securely hashed password.

  • Customer accounts as an optional feature; guest checkout can be simpler for the first version.

  • Role-based access for administrators and staff.

  • Secure session or token handling, login validation, and logout.

  • Never put passwords, JWT secrets, or database credentials in frontend code.

Payments

Start with cash on delivery, cash at pickup, or pay-at-counter if those fit the restaurant's business. You can add online payments later.

If you need online payment in Ethiopia, investigate a supported provider such as Telebirr or Chapa and confirm its current merchant onboarding requirements, API availability, fees, and settlement rules before implementation. Do not mark an order paid just because a customer returns to a success page; verify payment through the provider's trusted server-side confirmation mechanism.

Order security

  • Validate all input on the backend.

  • Recalculate prices and totals on the server.

  • Restrict who can cancel or update orders.

  • Prevent duplicate order submissions where possible.

  • Use rate limiting and appropriate authentication protections.

  • Keep secrets in environment variables and exclude .env from Git.

  • Validate image uploads and use a suitable image storage service for production.

11. Step-by-step development roadmap

Follow this order so that you do not spend time designing features that cannot work yet.

  1. Set up the project

    Install Node.js, VS Code, Git, and MongoDB Atlas or another accessible MongoDB deployment. Create the frontend and backend folders.

  2. Build the frontend design

    Create the navigation bar, homepage, menu cards, category filters, About page, Contact page, and responsive footer. Use temporary menu data initially.

  3. Build the backend

    Set up Express, TypeScript, environment variables, MongoDB connection, models, controllers, routes, and error handling.

  4. Connect the menu

    Fetch real menu items from MongoDB through the API. Build admin functions to create, update, remove, and disable menu items.

  5. Build the cart and checkout

    Support quantity changes, order types, customer details, input validation, and server-side total calculation.

  6. Implement order management

    Save orders in MongoDB and show them in the admin dashboard. Implement and validate the status transition rules.

  7. Add authentication and permissions

    Protect admin APIs, secure credentials, and test unauthorized access.

  8. Test the entire workflow

    Place an order as a customer, verify that staff can see it, update its status, and confirm that the customer can view the result.

  9. Deploy the application

    Deploy the frontend and backend, configure environment variables, database network access, CORS, production URLs, and HTTPS.

How to create the initial project

Open PowerShell in the folder where you want to keep the project:

powershell
mkdir "BW-JUICE-AND-BAR"
cd "BW-JUICE-AND-BAR"

npm create vite@latest frontend -- --template react-ts

mkdir backend
cd backend
npm init -y
npm install express mongoose cors dotenv bcrypt jsonwebtoken
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node @types/express @types/cors @types/bcrypt @types/jsonwebtoken
npx tsc --init

This creates the initial structure and installs backend packages. It does not yet create a complete working website. You will still need to configure TypeScript, package scripts, environment variables, database models, routes, and the frontend dependencies.

FULL-STACK DEVELOPMENT PROMPT: BW JUICE AND BAR RESTAURANT

Act as a senior full-stack software engineer, UI/UX designer, database architect, and security engineer. Build a complete, functional, responsive web-based restaurant ordering system named BW JUICE AND BAR RESTAURANT.

1. Technology Stack

Frontend

  • React with TypeScript and Vite.

  • React Router for navigation.

  • Pure CSS only.

  • Axios or Fetch API for backend communication.

  • Context API for shopping cart state.

  • Lucide React icons if needed.

Backend

  • Node.js with Express and TypeScript.

  • MongoDB with Mongoose.

  • JWT-based authentication where appropriate.

  • bcrypt for password hashing.

  • Environment variables for secrets and configuration.

  • Centralized error handling and request validation.

Do not use Tailwind CSS, Bootstrap, Material UI, or another CSS framework. Keep the frontend and backend in separate folders.

2. Customer Website

Create the following pages:

  1. Home

  2. Menu

  3. Product Details

  4. Shopping Cart

  5. Checkout

  6. Order Confirmation

  7. My Orders

  8. Login and optional Registration

  9. About Us

  10. Contact Us

The homepage must display the restaurant name and logo, attractive fruit juice and food photography, a hero section, Order Now button, popular products, categories, promotional sections, opening hours, contact information, and footer.

The menu must include configurable categories such as:

  • Fresh Juices

  • Smoothies and Milkshakes

  • Coffee and Tea

  • Breakfast and Snacks

  • Meals and Fast Food

  • Other Beverages

Each menu item must include its name, description, category, price, image, and availability. Add search, category filtering, and sorting.

3. Shopping Cart and Checkout

Implement a fully functional cart that supports:

  • Adding products.

  • Increasing and decreasing quantities.

  • Removing items.

  • Displaying subtotals and totals.

  • Handling unavailable products.

  • Preserving the cart during navigation.

Checkout must support dine-in, takeaway, and delivery where enabled by the restaurant.

Collect the appropriate customer name, phone number, table number or delivery address, and optional order instructions.

The backend must retrieve current product prices from MongoDB, validate quantities and availability, calculate totals, and save an order securely. Never trust prices supplied by the frontend.

Display an order number and confirmation after the order is successfully created.

4. Admin Dashboard

Create a separate protected admin interface with:

  • Dashboard Overview

  • Menu Management

  • Category Management

  • Order Management

  • Customer Management

  • Sales and Reports

  • Restaurant Settings

  • Admin Profile

  • Logout

The dashboard must display useful statistics, including order counts, pending orders, completed orders, sales totals, and popular menu items.

Administrators must be able to create, edit, delete, search, and disable menu items; upload or manage product images; manage categories; view order details; and update order statuses.

Use a controlled order lifecycle, for example:
Pending → Confirmed → Preparing → Ready → Completed.

Allow cancellation only when appropriate, record cancellation reasons, and prevent invalid status transitions.

Provide date filters for reports and CSV export where appropriate. Calculate sales from valid order records and distinguish completed sales from pending or cancelled orders.

5. Order and Payment Management

Store order items with snapshots of the product name, unit price, and quantity at the time of ordering.

Include:

  • Unique order number.

  • Customer contact details.

  • Order type.

  • Item subtotal.

  • Delivery fee where applicable.

  • Total amount.

  • Payment method.

  • Payment status.

  • Order status.

  • Creation and update timestamps.

Support configurable cash payment options initially. Keep online payment integration modular so a supported payment provider can be added later.

Never mark a payment successful based only on a frontend redirect. Verify online payments on the backend using the provider's trusted verification mechanism.

6. Database Models

Implement appropriate Mongoose models for:

  • User

  • Category

  • MenuItem

  • Order

  • Payment, if required

  • Review, if enabled

  • RestaurantSettings

Use validation, timestamps, appropriate indexes, and relationships or references where necessary.

Do not store plaintext passwords. Prevent unauthorized users from accessing protected information.

7. Backend API

Organize APIs under /api.

Public endpoints should support menu browsing, category browsing, and order creation.

Authentication endpoints should support login and logout/session handling as appropriate.

Protected admin endpoints should support:

  • Dashboard statistics.

  • Menu CRUD.

  • Category CRUD.

  • Order listing and status updates.

  • Customer administration.

  • Sales reports.

  • Restaurant settings.

Use controllers, routes, models, middleware, services, and configuration files. Return consistent JSON responses and appropriate HTTP status codes.

Validate incoming data, enforce permissions on the server, prevent unauthorized order modifications, and handle errors without exposing secrets.

8. Design Requirements

Create a premium, fresh, modern juice-bar restaurant design.

Use:

  • Orange as the primary accent.

  • Fresh green as a secondary accent.

  • White or warm cream backgrounds.

  • Dark, readable text.

  • High-quality food and juice images.

  • Responsive product cards.

  • Clear navigation and visible cart count.

  • Attractive but restrained hover effects.

  • Accessible forms and buttons.

  • Responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile layouts.

  • A consistent admin sidebar and dashboard layout.

Provide light and dark themes if they can be implemented cleanly.

9. Project Structure

Use separate frontend and backend directories.

The frontend should contain reusable components, pages, page-specific CSS, API services, cart state management, TypeScript types, and route configuration.

The backend should contain configuration, models, controllers, routes, middleware, services, utilities, and the server entry point.

Use clear filenames and maintainable code. Do not put the entire application in a single file.

10. Testing and Deployment

Provide:

  • .env.example files.

  • A complete .gitignore.

  • A README with setup instructions.

  • Safe database initialization and an optional seed script.

  • API testing instructions.

  • Error handling and loading states.

  • Empty states for menus and orders.

  • Form validation and success/error notifications.

  • Instructions for deploying the frontend to Vercel and the backend to Render.

Never commit .env, passwords, JWT secrets, database credentials, or other private information.

11. Development Instructions

Build the project incrementally, not as a large untested code dump.

First, provide the project folder structure and installation commands. Then implement the frontend, backend, database, cart, checkout, order management, and authentication in a logical sequence.

For every implementation step:

  1. State the exact file path.

  2. Provide complete code for the file.

  3. Explain where to run each command.

  4. Explain how to test the feature.

  5. Check imports, package dependencies, TypeScript types, API URLs, and environment variables.

  6. Fix errors before moving to the next feature.

Do not use fake API responses as if they were real database records. Temporary mock data may be used only during initial frontend development and must be replaced with real API integration.

The final result must be a working full-stack restaurant ordering system, not just a visual prototype. Clearly identify any feature that still requires configuration, credentials, or external services.

13. Decisions to make before you start

These choices affect the database, checkout, and business logic. Select your preferences below to establish the first version's requirements.

1. Which order types do you need?

2. Which payment method should the first version support?

3. How should customers access the system?

4. What currency should prices use?

5. Choose the visual style

My recommendation: build the menu, cart, checkout, and admin order management first. Test that a real order can travel from the customer's browser to MongoDB and appear in the admin dashboard before adding advanced features. That is the core of the business, and it must work reliably.
